opening.headline: Learn how to identify which tuning method fits your needs: fixing format, refining tone, and teaching criteria.
body: Tuning is one thing, but the learning signal given to the model is completely different depending on the method. There are ways to show exemplary responses, ways to compare two responses, and ways to provide scoring criteria, and each requires a different shape of the data.

In this class, we first point out that learning involves modifying weights to reduce loss, compare the learning signals and data formats of SFT, DPO, and RFT, and look at distillation to create a small model from the output of a large model. Next, we check the training/validation split, overfitting signals, tuning best practices, and basic model dependencies, and follow the three cases with explanations.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the difference between supervised learning, preference learning, and reinforcement learning-based tuning
You can distinguish between methods suitable for learning format fixation, tone, and judgment criteria.
Explain that learning is modifying weights to reduce loss and state the purpose of SFT.
RFT can explain the risk of learning a grader's weaknesses and how to check for regression in existing capabilities after tuning.

screens.title: I decided to do some tuning, but what is the method?
screens.lead: First, read three meeting notes from the team that decided to tune in. Read this wondering if the three demands will be resolved in the same way.

visual.alt: A scene with three meeting notes side by side, each with a question mark arrow leading to a different tuning method.
labels: Fixed the answer format to always be the same JSON structure
In a more polite and concise tone
Familiarize yourself with the criteria for determining risk in contract provisions

paragraphs: The team running the customer-facing bot decided, “Now let’s tune the model.” The meeting notes state three demands: First, I want to ensure that the answer format is always fixed to the same JSON structure. Second, even if I say the same thing, I want to change it to a more polite and concise tone. Third, I would like the model to learn the criteria for judging whether a contract provision is risky.

Although all three needs are referred to by one word, “tuning,” the shape of the data required and learning method are different. The format can be done by showing a set model response, but the tone is difficult to write down as a rule, and the judgment criteria must be scored by an expert to be meaningful.

If you choose the wrong method, you can create data for several weeks and not meet your needs. For example, to teach tone, you create hundreds of model responses with rules in mind, but the results don't change much.

In this lesson, we compare three approaches: Supervised Learning Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT). We take a look at each of the three methods in turn to see what learning signals they use, what the data looks like, and what needs they fit.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What would the data look like for each of the three needs: fixing format, improving tone, and learning criteria? After class, you will be able to answer with evidence.

screens.outro: Let me think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever written a long list of rules in a prompt and ended up breaking the format in some calls?
items.answer: Describing the rules in writing is a way to expect the model to understand and follow the rules. Breaking the format means that even though there are rules, they are not followed consistently. In this case, it is appropriate to teach the child by showing him/her many examples of correct responses.

items.prompt: Have you ever known “this answer is better than that answer” but found it difficult to write it down as a rule?
items.answer: What to focus on in your tone or summary is more of a preference than a rule. Putting two answers side by side makes it easy to choose, but it's hard to write down the reasons as a rule. To turn these sensations into learning signals, we need data to compare responses.

items.prompt: Has there ever been a time when human experts agreed on the same answer, but the model couldn't follow that judgment?
items.answer: If the correct answer is a consensus judgment among experts, you can define criteria for scoring how good the answer is. There is a way to use the scoring criteria as a learning signal. The more reasoning the judgment itself requires, the more effective it becomes.

items.prompt: How will this lesson connect the three scenes?
items.answer: This lesson explains why each of the three scenes leads to a different tuning approach. The format is to follow model responses, preference is to compare responses, and the judgment criteria is to use scoring criteria.

screens.outro: First, let's compare what learning signals each of the three methods uses.

screens.title: What Learning Does: Modifying Weights to Reduce Loss
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and follow the tuning learning process step by step. Just look at the flow without using any formulas.

visual.alt: A cycle diagram that repeats the process of looking at examples, making predictions, measuring losses, and adjusting weights.
labels: The model predicts words one by one
Loss: How far are you from your goals?
Repetition: Going through the entire data once takes 1 epoch.
Full weights or adapters (small additions) only

steps.title: The starting point is the already learned weights
steps.body: Tuning is not about teaching a model from scratch. This involves starting from a model whose weights have already been established through pre-learning, and further modifying the weights using a small amount of data. So, you can add new actions while maintaining the existing abilities, or on the other hand, if you modify it too harshly, the existing abilities may be shaken.

steps.title: Look at examples and predict the next word
steps.body: One training example consists of a prompt and a target response. The model repeats the task of assigning probabilities to the next word (token), one by one, given the prompt and the first part of the target response. If the target response is “within 14 days of purchase,” then the probability of “after” coming after “purchase” is calculated.

steps.title: Measure the amount of deviation in terms of loss.
steps.body: Loss is a single number that indicates how far the model's predictions are from the target. If the model gives a high probability for each word of the target response, the loss is small, and if it gives a low probability, the loss is large. Learning proceeds using this number as a compass. If the loss goes down, it means the model is tracking the target better.

steps.title: Adjust the weight little by little
steps.body: We modify the weights very slightly in a way that reduces the loss. The learning rate is the value that determines how much to fix at one time. If it is too big, even the abilities you already have will be shaken, and if it is too small, there will be little change. These modifications are repeated for numerous examples, and one look at the entire training data is called an epoch.

steps.title: SFT lets you repeat model responses word for word
steps.body: The target response for supervised learning fine-tuning is a human-written exemplar response. We define the loss so that, given the preceding words, the probability of the next word in the exemplar response increases. As a result, responses with the same format and tone are more likely to occur. This is why SFT is suitable for determining a single standard response, for example, fixing the JSON format.

steps.title: You can fix it all or just some of it.
steps.body: Fixing all weights is computationally and storage expensive. The adapter method fixes the existing weights as is and only learns small additional weights to place on top of them. LoRA, a representative method, has been reported to significantly reduce the number of numbers to learn while producing quality similar to that of a complete fix (Hu et al., 2021). In this case, the extras can only be spent on the base model.

steps.title: DPO and RFT are also the same framework.
steps.body: DPO and RFT have the same framework of iteration to change the weights little by little, but they differ only on what basis they are modified. DPO increases the probability of a good response and decreases the probability of a less good response, while RFT improves the response in the direction of producing more responses with high values ​​given by the grader. The next screen compares these three signals side by side.

screens.outro: Now that we know what the learning cycle is, let's compare what each of the three methods sees and learns.

ext.title: Hu et al. (2021), LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

screens.title: Three types of learning signals: exemplars, comparisons, and rewards.
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what the three tuning methods see and learn.

tabs.label: SFT
tabs.body: Supervised Fine-Tuning presents you with a pair of prompts and exemplary responses, and has the model mimic those responses word-by-word. Human-made “correct” responses are often used. In one line, it is “Say it like this.” It is appropriate to choose one standard response.

tabs.label: DPO
tabs.body: Direct Preference Optimization gives a pair of good and less good answers to a prompt and trains the prompt to produce more good answers. In one line: “This is better.” You can learn more subjective people's preferences. The principle is as follows. Without creating a separate compensation model, adjust the weights to increase the probability of a good response and lower the probability of a less good response, but tie them so that they do not deviate too much from the model at the time of starting tuning (baseline model). DPO is a method that first learns a reward model by comparing human preferences and reduces reinforcement learning (RLHF) to simpler learning (Rafailov et al., 2023).

tabs.label: RFT
tabs.body: In Reinforcement Fine-Tuning, a human-defined grader assigns a value to each candidate response instead of a fixed model answer. Training repeats the cycle of creating multiple candidate responses, scoring them with a grader, and gradually adjusting the model weights so that more high-value responses are produced. In one line, it is “I will grade you based on this standard.”

tabs.label: Name of each provider
tabs.body: Although the names and settings are different for each provider, the same three categories are used. These include supervised tuning with labeled data, preference tuning that teaches preferences from response pairs, and reinforcement learning tuning with user-defined reward functions. Don't get caught up in the name; start by checking whether the learning cue is a model response, comparison, or reward.

screens.outro: Now that we know the difference between signals, let's see for ourselves how the data looks different.

ext.title: Rafailov et al. (2023), Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model

screens.title: View three data formats side by side
screens.lead: Take turns reading each part of the code and the explanation on the right. All three methods write JSONL files, with one complete JSON structure per line. The example below is divided into lines for easy reading.

notes.note: SFT one line. Place the assistant's model response after the user message. It has to be exactly in the format the operation expects, and if the key name is different in each case, the model learns that shake as well.

DPO one line. There is a question in input, and preferred_output and non_preferred_output are paired. Both are final assistant messages and only have one turn of dialogue. If it is misaligned, it will not be accepted as training data.

RFT one line. There is no model response, but fields such as compliant that are referenced by the prompt and grader are included. Candidate responses from the model are sampled during training and scored by a grader. If the field name is different from the grader's reference representation, it will not be graded.
For all three methods, files are uploaded separately for training and verification purposes. Verification files should be stored separately and not used for learning to check for overfitting.

screens.outro: Now that we have looked at the shape of the data, we will organize which needs fit which method.

data.notes: Supervised tuning is an appropriate method when there are well-defined tasks and labeled data. Typical examples include classification, summarization, extractive Q&A, and chat. The first question that determines the method is whether there are labels, only comparisons, or only scoring criteria can be defined. DPO is suitable for learning subjective preferences such as tone of voice, and RFT is suitable for inference that requires expert judgment. The fourth column of the table shows the inputs you must have to get started with each method.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at a separate method of targeting efficiency: distillation.

screens.title: Distillation: Results from a large model into a small model
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and follow the distillation process step by step.

steps.title: Refine prompts for large models
steps.body: Distillation is a technique derived from the classic idea of transferring the knowledge of a large model into a small, easy-to-deploy model. Hinton et al. in 2015 summarized the method of condensing the knowledge of a large model into a single, small model. Here, we will cover a form of tuning a smaller model by creating training data for SFT using the output of the larger model. First, refine the prompt until the larger model performs well on the evaluation criteria. The evaluation made at this stage becomes the basis for future comparisons.

steps.title: Gather the output of a large model
steps.body: Gather the output of a large model with refined prompts. If you already have response records accumulated while operating a service, you can utilize them. Input prompts along with output must be paired together to form learning examples.

steps.title: Choose only the output that meets your standards
steps.body: Among the collected outputs, only those that meet the criteria are selected to create a dataset. This selection determines distillation quality, as not all outputs from larger models are as good. The criteria uses the same evaluation set and scoring method used to evaluate a large model.

steps.title: SFT tuning a small model
steps.body: A smaller, cheaper model is tuned using SFT using selected data. The learning method is the same as a regular SFT, the difference is that the data is obtained from the output of a large model rather than from humans.

steps.title: Evaluate the results
steps.body: The goal is to have a small model that performs similarly to a larger model at a specific task. The same evaluation checks whether costs and delays are reduced and quality is maintained compared to larger models. Distillation is a method that aims for efficiency rather than accuracy.

screens.outro: Let's look at the concept of partitioning, which is essential when writing training data.

ext.title: Hinton, Vinyals, Dean (2015), Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network

screens.title: Learning/Verification Splitting and Overfitting Signals
screens.lead: Move the slider to change how much learning progresses. The explanation of how the loss on the training side and the performance on the validation side change at each stage changes. The explanation below changes each time the selection value changes.

stops.body: The loss on the learning side goes down quickly and the performance on the verification side also improves. This is the section where the model learns generalizable rules. An epoch is one walk through the entire training data, usually multiple epochs. In this section, the two curves move together, so it makes sense to continue learning.

Both curves improve, but the improvement on the verification side begins to decrease. Checkpoints created around this time are often the best candidates. A checkpoint is a saved model at a specific point during training. If you save each epoch, you can later go back to the best version of the model.

The loss on the training side continues to go down, but the performance on the validation side stagnates or deteriorates. This is a sign of overfitting, where the model has started to memorize training data instead of generalizable rules. If you see this point, you can use the previous checkpoint.

To see this signal, you need to split the data into a training set and a validation set, with the validation set set aside for training. In RFT, the prompt data is divided into training and verification purposes, and verification indicators are monitored during learning. The size and composition of the validation set is also meaningful if it resembles the distribution of the operational input.

screens.outro: Now, we will summarize best practices for good tuning.

screens.title: Tuning Best Practices: Quality, Quantity, and Hyperparameters
screens.lead: By selecting and expanding each item, you can see what to check before and during tuning.

items.title: Do the evaluation first
items.body: You don't start out with no way to determine if your tuned model is better than the base model. Evaluation is the starting point and success criterion for tuning. This evaluation can be done through code scoring, which compares directly to the correct answer, or model scoring, where the scoring model makes the decisions.

items.title: starting scale
items.body: The minimum number of cases is 10, with improvement usually seen in 50 to 100 cases. First, check the effectiveness with 50 well-made cases, and increase the number of cases when it is effective. If there is no change at 50, reconsider the task or prompt before adding data. Research shows that response format and style can be learned from just a small number of high-quality examples. The LIMA study achieved good results even after supervised learning with 1,000 carefully selected prompt/response pairs, and interpreted that most of the knowledge comes from prior learning and the small amount of data is used to tailor the response method (Zhou et al., 2023).

items.title: quality
items.body: Add examples that directly demonstrate the remaining failures, and check existing examples for the same syntax or logic issues. A small amount of high-quality data is better than a large amount of low-quality data.

items.title: balance
items.body: If 60% of the training data is “unanswerable” but only 5% is operational, the model will reject too much. Fit the distribution of training data to the distribution of operations.

items.title: consistency
items.body: If there is only 70% agreement between authors, it is difficult for the model to exceed that level. The examples must contain all the information needed to respond so the model does not learn hallucinations.

items.title: hyperparameter
items.body: Values that can be adjusted include number of epochs, learning rate multiplier, and batch size. First, start with the default values ​​and change them little by little while looking at the evaluation results. If you change several values ​​at once, you won't know what has the effect, so it's better to change them one by one and compare them.

items.title: Identify regression of existing abilities (regression assessment)
items.body: Tuning involves modifying weights, so training with a narrow range of data may reduce performance in areas that were not studied. Research has shown that forgetting previously held abilities while continuously fine-tuning the model (catastrophic forgetting) is commonly observed in models from 1B to 7B scale (Luo et al., 2023). So, separate from the evaluation set of the target task, we have a separate regression evaluation set that checks what we were already doing well before tuning. Include things you are good at, such as general questions and answers, other types of requests, and requests that should be rejected, and compare the same set before and after tuning. If you see a large drop in regression evaluation even if your target task has improved, expand the data range or reduce the amount of training.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's look at what you need to know when operating a tuned model.

ext.title: Zhou et al. (2023), LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment
Luo et al. (2023), An Empirical Study of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning

screens.title: Tuning model serving and base model dependence
screens.lead: Select the “While the base model is in service” and “After the base model goes down” buttons alternately to compare how the tuning models change. After checking both states, consider why you should keep your data as an asset.

states.label: While the base model is in service
states.body: Tuned models are built on top of a specific base model and can only be used for inference while that base model is in service. When tuning using the adapter method, the weights of the base model are left as is and only a small addition is learned on top of it, so this addition can only be used in conjunction with the base model. The advantage of using an adapter is that it is easy to utilize the existing basic model serving environment. There is also continuous tuning, which involves adding cases or epochs to an already tuned model and then refining it. At this time, you can call, evaluate, and operate the tuning model just like a regular model. However, always keep a record of which base model the object of the call is built on.

states.label: After the basic model goes down
states.body: If the basic model is lowered, the tuning model created above it will no longer be usable. Therefore, changing the base model means retraining and re-evaluating the tuning model. To reduce this burden, you should keep your training data and evaluation sets as assets. Then you can re-tune even if the model changes. When moving to a new base model, we retrain it on the same training data and compare it to the previous model on the same evaluation set. This is because if the basic model changes, the results may change even with the same data.

screens.outro: Now let's explain the three cases.

screens.title: Commentary 1: Format fixation to SFT
screens.lead: The instructor explains the first note step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The customer-facing bot emits a different JSON key name for each call. Sometimes I write `intent`, sometimes I write `category`, so the code that receives and processes the response keeps breaking. Each time the format is broken, either a human will need to fix it manually or retry logic will be required.

steps.title: judgment
steps.body: SFT is correct because it is a “say this” type where there is only one standard response. What the model needs is not a standard for judgment, but the experience of seeing the same type of response over and over again. When fixing the output format, the basic rule is to think of SFT first.

steps.title: data
steps.body: First, we create around 50 pairs of actual inquiries and correct JSON responses. It is exactly the same as the format used in operation. If the key names, order, and value notation are different for each case, the model will learn the difference, so people writing the cases must follow the same rules.

steps.title: verification
steps.body: Some are set aside and not used for learning. Compare format compliance with the same validation set before and after tuning, and increase cases when it works. The metrics compared in the validation set are the percentage of JSON that is parsed correctly and the percentage that has all required keys.

steps.title: Why not a DPO
steps.body: DPO is ideal for teaching “better than” preferences over formal rules. This problem, which has only one answer format, requires too much effort to create comparison pairs. Problems that can be solved in an easy way must be solved in an easy way. Conversely, if you use RFT to fix the format, you have to create a new grader first.

screens.outro: Next, let’s look at an example of teaching tone.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Tone preference goes to DPO
screens.lead: Selecting the highlighted passages in the comparison pairs below will reveal points to keep in mind when creating DPO data.

data.text:
Question: How cold is it in San Francisco today?  
Good response: It's not as cold in San Francisco today as expected. Morning clouds will clear and sunshine will come, followed by The highest temperature is about 20 degrees and the lowest temperature is about 14 degrees..  
Less good response: It's cold in San Francisco today, It's not particularly cold.  
Learning setup: DPO, Beta as a value between 0 and 2 specified

marks.span: The highest temperature is about 20 degrees and the lowest temperature is about 14 degrees.
marks.note: A good response will give you weather readings. If the two responses contain different amounts of information, the model may learn the difference in information rather than tone, so comparison pairs should be made so that both contain the same information.

The less good answers aren't wrong, but they're stiff and lack information. It's cumbersome to write "include numbers" as a rule, but when you compare two responses, it's easy to tell which is better. This is why DPO is right.

marks.span: Beta as a value between 0 and 2
marks.note: beta is a DPO-specific hyperparameter that determines how strictly the new model will adhere to its previous behavior. High values ​​result in conservative learning that sticks to existing behavior, while low values ​​result in aggressive learning that moves more toward new preferences.

DPO data learns only one-turn conversations, consisting of one question and one response. Both good and less good responses should be the last assistant message. If the conversation has multiple turns, data transformation is required.

screens.outro: In the following commentary, we will look at RFT that teaches judgment criteria.

screens.title: Commentary 3: The judgment standard is RFT, but there are conditions.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the solution will unfold. Five questions to check whether risk judgment of contract provisions can be taught with RFT.

items.prompt: How does RFT teach judgment criteria?
items.answer: Determining whether a provision is dangerous requires reasoning, and the correct judgment is determined by expert standards. In RFT, when the model creates multiple candidate responses, a grader scores each one, and learns to produce more responses with higher values. So, how well the grader holds professional standards determines the result.

items.prompt: Check 1: Do experts working independently arrive at the same answer?
items.answer: RFT requires expert raters to agree on an ideal output. If the answers are different among experts, there is no standard for graders to follow and the task must be redefined.

items.prompt: Checks 2 and 3: Can the work be graded by a grader, but not by taking a photo?
items.answer: The task must be gradable with the grader options provided by the API. Also, if you can get a high value even if you guess by luck, the learning signal becomes noise. Therefore, we design it to be difficult to take by increasing the number of options into subcategories or changing multiple choice questions to descriptive answers.

items.prompt: Check 4: What should the evaluation results be like before tuning?
items.answer: The value of the evaluation before tuning should be dispersed around the middle, rather than clustering at the lowest or highest ends. If all are wrong, there are no successful cases for improvement; if all are correct, there is no room for further improvement. A dispersed state around the middle indicates the presence of material for enhancement.

items.prompt: Check 5: Is the model learning the grader's weaknesses?
items.answer: RFT causes the model to learn to generate more responses that receive high scores from the grader, thereby optimizing not what we truly want, but rather the mechanism by which the grader assigns scores. When there are gaps or flaws in the evaluation criteria, responses that exploit these weaknesses receive higher scores and are reinforced—this is known as reward hacking. For example, if a grader assigns high scores when the word "dangerous" appears, the model might learn to simply repeat that word without actually evaluating the content (as a hypothetical example). Two methods can be used to detect such issues: first, manually reviewing response samples that received high scores to verify whether their content is actually accurate; second, comparing the model's performance on a separate evaluation set using graders or human evaluators based on different criteria. If the model's training scores increase while the separate evaluation scores remain stagnant or decline, this signals that the model has learned to exploit a flaw.

data.notes: In either case, the evaluation set comes first. We divide training and validation data, watch for overfitting with checkpoints, and prioritize quality and representativeness of cases over quantity. Although the names are different for each provider, supervised tuning, preferred tuning, and reinforcement learning tuning are distinguished by the same criteria. The rules in the table are a starting point, and in practice small-scale pilot studies are often used to confirm the method.

screens.outro: I will organize the concepts up to this point into cards.

screens.title: Concept map revisited
screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate key concepts related to tuning. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

cards.back: The format and classification are anchored by pairs of prompts and model responses. Teach “Say it this way.” Example: Fixed JSON key name for a customer-facing bot.

Teach tone and preferences by comparing good and less good responses to the same question. Both sides of a comparison pair must contain the same information. Example: Teaching a warm tone that includes weather figures as a preference.

This is a method of reinforcing responses with high values based on the value assigned by the grader. Fits complex inferences that can be agreed upon by experts and graded by graders. Example: When determining whether a contract provision is risky.

This is a method of SFTing a small model using the good output of a large model as data. The goal is to reduce costs and delays. Example: Creating a smaller, cheaper model from the classification results of a larger model.

cards.front: Overfitting and relying on default models
cards.back: Monitor overfitting with validation splits and checkpoints. Tuned models depend on the base model, so they must be retrained and evaluated if the base model changes.

screens.outro: Now, let's outline the criteria for translating this concept into a business plan.

screens.title: What to check when planning tuning
screens.lead: Let's group the contents of this class into the order used when creating a tuning plan. Read it slowly.

paragraphs: If you decide to do tuning, first set up an evaluation and decide what type of training signal you want to teach the model. Consider SFT if there is a set model response, DPO if it is easy to compare good and bad responses, and RFT if a grader can grade a judgment that experts agree on.

Once the method is decided, data is created. We start with around 50 well-made cases, increase them if they are effective, structure them to resemble the operational distribution, and align the standards among those writing the cases. Some are set aside for verification purposes.

After learning is complete, check the performance and checkpoints on the verification side to check for overfitting. When putting it into production, plan that the tuning model depends on the base model, and keep the training data and evaluation set as assets. If your goal is to reduce costs, consider distillation.

Lastly, once you decide on a method, you don't have to stick to it. You can also apply them sequentially, first formatting with SFT and then refining the tone with DPO. In either case, the key is to check for improvement at every step with the same set of assessments.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Regardless of the method used, data is more important in terms of quality and representativeness than quantity. A small number of high-quality examples is better than a large number of poor ones.

checks.q: What is the most appropriate meaning of "loss" in SFT learning?
options: The sum of satisfaction ratings given by a person for each response
This is a number that indicates how much the model's prediction deviates from the model response, and the weight is adjusted in a decreasing direction.

glossary.def: Supervised tuning that trains a model with prompt and exemplar response pairs.
This method teaches preferences for pairs of good and less good responses to the same prompt.
This is a reinforcement fine-tuning that produces more high-value responses based on the value assigned by the grader.
This is a technique for tuning a smaller model using data created from the output of a larger model.
This is a phenomenon in which verification performance stagnates or worsens due to learning data being memorized.
It is a number that indicates how much the model's prediction deviates from the target response. Learning is an iteration of adjusting the weight in the direction of decreasing this value.

misconceptions.myth: Tuning is always better with more data.
misconceptions.fact: Quality and representation come first. A small amount of good cases is better than a large amount of bad cases, so first check the effect with around 50 cases and then increase it.

misconceptions.myth: RFT is upward compatible with SFT.
misconceptions.fact: RFT is only effective on tasks where experts agree on the same answers and can be graded by a grader. For tasks where the correct answer is known, such as format fixation, SFT is simpler and more appropriate.

misconceptions.myth: Once a tuned model is created, it can be used forever.
misconceptions.fact: Tuning models depend on a specific base model. Data and evaluation sets must be archived because they will need to be retrained and evaluated if the underlying model changes.

misconceptions.myth: Tuning improves only the target task, while other abilities remain the same.
misconceptions.fact: Modifying weights with narrow data may reduce performance in untrained areas. Before tuning, you should have a separate regression evaluation set containing what you were doing well and compare before and after.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: SFT uses model responses, DPO uses response comparison, and RFT uses the grader's scoring value as a learning signal. All are learning methods that gradually change the weights based on loss or reward.

SFT is suitable for format fixation and classification, DPO is suitable for tone and preference, and RFT is suitable for complex reasoning that can define grading criteria. However, RFT must directly check the responses that received high values to ensure that the grader's loopholes are not learned.
Distillation is a method of reducing costs by SFTing a small model with the good output of a large model.

Overfitting is monitored through validation splits and checkpoints, quality and representativeness of data are prioritized over quantity, and after tuning, regression evaluation is performed to check whether existing capabilities have deteriorated.
Tuning models rely on the base model, so they keep data and evaluation sets as assets.
